name: Wendy Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. We keep this confidential. What is a normal lineworker day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am fifty-eight and still learning the electricity company’s power line work. I have a vocational certificate, but I am a junior on the crew, usually getting the materials ready, watching the isolation check and helping repair a span under someone more experienced. I like seeing a dark street come back, and I dislike being rushed when I am not yet sure of a fault. My partner and I have grown children, and retirement is closer than I feel ready for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a little AI paperwork does not mend a line, and the crew still needs to train people properly. I would keep doing the preparation and repairs they trust me with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I cannot call the money safe just because AI stalls. My pay is low for this work, we have less than one month saved, and there are few other lineworker posts nearby. A quiet year for AI will not make my junior lineworker wage fill an empty savings account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep taking my junior shifts and ask the crew lead to show me the isolation sheet each morning. This month my partner and I would stop buying takeaway meals after late shifts and put any money left toward the next bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, the same as before the AI question. A quiet technology year does not make a thin savings account bigger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill worries you after a late shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The heating and food bills sit closest to the edge for us. If we skip takeaway, I would put that money toward whichever one is due first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep asking to see the isolation sheet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am still learning and cannot afford a careless mistake on a live line. The crew lead can tell me where my preparation does not match the actual job.

say: **Routine** AI cannot replace junior lineworker practice or safe preparation.
I would **keep** asking the crew lead to explain isolation checks.
think: **Low** pay and savings below one month already strain our household.
**Few** nearby line jobs make another shift hard to replace.
do: **Keep** junior line shifts and review isolation sheet with crew lead.
**Stop** buying takeaway after late shifts and cover the next household bill.
feel: **Anxious** about ordinary costs despite little AI change.
S0.quote: A quiet year for AI will not make my junior lineworker wage fill an empty savings account.
fieldNote: Her **fear** is rooted in current pay and savings, not an invented AI cut.
She **remains** a learner at fifty-eight despite the long work history her age might suggest.

steps.text: Keep junior shifts and review isolation sheet with crew lead
Stop takeaway purchases after late shifts to cover household bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that faster booking is fine if a real dispatcher still answers when a work order is wrong. The union should make sure apprentices and junior workers get enough paid time to learn the physical repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Planning work may thin out before the line work does, but a tighter schedule could make a slower junior worker look expendable. I cannot retire on less than a month of savings, and I do not use AI tools to make myself look quick. A scheduling screen can move my start time, but it cannot teach me a safe power line repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep a notebook of work orders that leave too little time for a safe setup. In the first year I would take the examples to our union steward with a request for protected paid training hours, while keeping my assigned repairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my hours, though I still think the crew needs hands. I cannot learn faster because a screen has moved a start time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would go in your notebook?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would note the work order, setup time, the isolation check and what the crew lead had to correct. I do not want to complain about a clock without showing the missing steps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the union steward to secure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for paid time beside an experienced lineworker on difficult jobs, with no penalty for asking a safety question. I am not asking for a course on a screen.

say: A **real** dispatcher should answer when automated booking sends a wrong work order.
I would **ask** the union to protect paid field learning for junior workers.
think: **Tighter** schedules might make a slower learner lose hours even while crews remain useful.
**Retirement** is not affordable from our thin savings, and I do not use AI tools.
do: **Record** work orders that shortchange safe setup time.
**Bring** examples to union steward for protected paid field training.
**Keep** assigned junior repairs while asking for safe time.
feel: **Anxious** about hours and the pace of learning.
S1.quote: A scheduling screen can move my start time, but it cannot teach me a safe power line repair.
fieldNote: She **fears** a real hours squeeze because she is junior and still learning.
Her **requested** training is paid practice with a worker, not a software course.

steps.text: Record unsafe setup estimates on junior work orders
Bring examples to union steward for paid field learning

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my union that full thinking AI by 2028 may take dispatch first, and capable line robots around 2031 may take much of the junior preparation work. The company should guarantee paid transition time before reducing field hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At sixty in 2028 I might still be learning the trade, and at sixty-three when robots arrive I expect the junior preparation shifts I need for retirement to be cut first. We have almost no savings and few nearby jobs; if my pay goes, I do not know how we cover food. A line robot may reach the pole in 2031, but my grocery bill will arrive long before retirement money does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week my partner and I would list the bills and cut our paid television package. Before 2028 I would ask the union to bargain for a written hours floor and paid training for junior crews, and in the first year after full thinking AI arrives I would ask our grown children for temporary grocery help only if my shifts actually fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, and I have lain awake counting the weeks a missed wage would leave us. I would not pretend a new machine is my personal chance to get rich.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your grown children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the shifts fell, I would tell them the actual gap and ask whether they could cover one grocery trip while we seek other work. I would not assume they can afford it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which training would you ask the company to pay for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for supervised line inspection practice that suits my certificate and current skill. I would not sign up for an unpaid course without an offered job at the end.

say: **Thinking** AI may reach dispatch by 2028, with robots taking hands-on tasks around 2031.
I would **push** for paid transition time and a written floor on junior hours.
think: **Junior** preparation shifts are likely to be cut when robots arrive as I reach sixty-three.
With **almost** no savings and few local jobs, household food costs become frightening.
do: **Cancel** paid television package after listing household bills.
**Ask** union to bargain for junior hours floor and paid transition training.
**Ask** grown children for one grocery trip only if shifts actually fall.
feel: **Alarmed** and losing sleep over a possible large income gap.
S2.quote: A line robot may reach the pole in 2031, but my grocery bill will arrive long before retirement money does.
fieldNote: The **fast** timeline intersects with her junior status at sixty-three and thin savings.
**Family** help is conditional on lost shifts and her children’s ability to assist.

steps.text: Cancel paid television package after listing bills
Ask union to bargain for junior hours floor and paid training
Ask grown children for grocery help if shifts fall and they can afford it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say full thinking AI in 2031 changes the office first and capable robots around 2034 reach our hands later. I would ask the company and union to plan a paid bridge for older junior workers before field tasks disappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At sixty-three when thinking AI arrives, I may still need wages; at sixty-six for robots, I cannot assume any retirement payment will cover us. Five years gives me time to check the figures, but not a reason to leave a job now. A retirement date written on paper will not replace the junior lineworker wage in my kitchen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would request a written estimate of my available retirement income from the plan administrator and lay it beside our household bills. If the company posts paid supervised inspection training at wages we can live on, I would enroll before 2031; otherwise I would keep taking line shifts and ask the union to protect them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but the longer notice lets me count rather than guess. I would feel better with an actual income figure and paid work options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What number would make stopping line shifts possible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I cannot name it until the administrator gives me an estimate and we add up food, housing and health costs. If the gap remains, I will keep working as long as I can safely do the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn inspection from a screen alone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would need supervised practice on real lines and enough pay during training to cover our regular bills.

say: The **company** and union should plan a paid bridge before robots reach field work around 2034.
I would **not** leave line work on a retirement guess.
think: At **sixty-six** I may still need wages because savings are below one month.
**More** notice lets me compare a real retirement estimate with household bills.
do: **Request** written retirement income estimate and compare it with bills.
**Enroll** before 2031 if company posts paid supervised inspection training with living wages.
**Keep** line shifts if paid training or adequate retirement income is absent.
feel: **Anxious** but helped by time to get actual figures and paid options.
S3.quote: A retirement date written on paper will not replace the junior lineworker wage in my kitchen.
fieldNote: She **asks** for financial facts rather than claiming a guaranteed pension or retirement age.
**Retraining** depends on a posted, paid, hands-on program that covers bills; asking for retirement figures alone does not change her work.

steps.text: Enroll before 2031 if posted supervised inspection training pays household bills
Keep junior line shifts if paid training or adequate retirement income is absent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues that full thinking AI in 2036 and capable robots around 2039 gives workers years to settle fair retirement and training terms. I would rather keep learning safe repairs than be pushed out at a fixed age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At sixty-eight for thinking AI and seventy-one for the robots, I might already have stopped climbing if my health and income allow. But with almost no savings now, I cannot promise that outcome, and my partner would still need household money. A line robot arriving when I am seventy-one does not promise my partner and me a paid retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my current shifts and review my retirement income estimate each year against our expenses. During the first year after 2036, if the actual income covers the bills and I can safely leave, I would finish the electricity company job; if it does not, I would request a paid ground support duty rather than keep climbing beyond what I can manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious rather than panicked, because ten years is time to ask for terms. I still cannot relax about money we have not saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would ground support mean on a repair day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could prepare materials, check the site list and keep a record of the isolation while a qualified worker handles the climb. I would ask for a written paid assignment before relying on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the retirement figure never covers the bills?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep working within what I can safely do and ask the company and union for a paid ground role. Our grown children have their own lives, so I would not build a ten-year plan around their money.

say: A **decade** allows real retirement and ground-duty planning before robots reach lines around 2039.
I would **resist** being pushed out by age alone.
think: At **sixty-eight** or seventy-one I may still need wages because current savings are very thin.
**Health** and actual retirement income determine whether I can stop climbing.
do: **Keep** junior shifts and compare retirement estimate with bills each year.
**Leave** line work after 2036 only if actual income covers household costs.
**Request** paid ground support duty if income falls short and climbing becomes unsafe.
feel: **Anxious** about unsaved money, though able to use the longer timeline.
S4.quote: A line robot arriving when I am seventy-one does not promise my partner and me a paid retirement.
fieldNote: She **avoids** assuming a statutory retirement age or a guaranteed pension amount.
**Leaving** the job depends on adequate income; ground support depends on safety and a paid assignment.

steps.text: Keep junior shifts and review retirement estimate against bills annually
Leave line job after 2036 only if retirement income covers bills
Request paid ground support if income falls short and climbing unsafe

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I could be sixty-three when line robots arrive around 2031, still needing junior wages with almost nothing saved. A written hours floor, paid supervised training and a clear retirement income estimate would help. The power line company cannot ask an older learner to live on an unpaid promise.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask how someone my age got this far without a cushion while still learning the job. Low pay and gaps between shifts have not left much after household bills. I need work that is safe and paid, not a lecture about being more flexible.

headlineQuote: The power line company cannot ask an older learner to live on an unpaid promise.
portrait: **Wendy** is a fifty-eight-year-old junior lineworker with a vocational certificate who still learns supervised repair and isolation work.
Her **partner** and grown children are part of her life, but low pay and less than one month saved make retirement uncertain.
**Few** local lineworker posts and no AI experience leave her exposed to schedule pressure even before capable robots arrive.
She **asks** her union for paid practice and hours protection, and would leave only when actual retirement income covers household costs.
biggestWorry: **AGI** by 2028 could bring capable line robots around 2031 when she is sixty-three and still needs junior wages.
whatWouldHelp: A **written** hours floor, paid supervised training and a real retirement income estimate would let her plan safely.
